opus-5.5.text:
It's a real problem, and I think it's underappreciated. When you evaluate a model behind an API, you're implicitly assuming that the thing you measured on Tuesday is the same thing someone else measures on Friday. If the provider swaps out weights, changes the system prompt, adjusts safety filters, or tweaks decoding defaults without saying so, that assumption quietly breaks. And at that point it's not entirely clear what object your scientific claim is even about.

The first casualty is reproducibility. A paper says "model X achieves this accuracy on this benchmark," and a year later someone tries to replicate it and gets a different number. Is that because the original work had a flaw, because the replication did something different, or because the model itself changed underneath? You often can't tell. That ambiguity erodes trust in the whole literature, not just one result.

The second issue is longitudinal claims. People want to say things like "capability on reasoning tasks is improving over time" or "this model got worse at coding." Those are interesting questions, but if versioning is opaque, you can't cleanly separate real changes in the model from changes in the serving stack, the prompt wrapper, or even load-dependent behavior. You end up attributing effects to the wrong cause.

Third, it complicates comparisons. If you're comparing two systems and one was silently updated midway through your evaluation, your comparison is confounded. That matters a lot when the results feed into decisions: procurement, policy, safety assessments.

So what can you claim? I think the honest framing is that many evaluations of closed, hosted models are really measurements of a service at a point in time, not of a fixed artifact. That's still useful, but it should be stated that way. Practically, that means logging timestamps, recording whatever version identifiers are exposed, saving raw outputs, and, where possible, including some canary or anchor tasks that let you detect drift. On the provider side, the ask is pretty modest: stable, pinned versions, clear changelogs, and deprecation notices. Without that, we're doing something closer to field observation than controlled experiment, and our claims should be calibrated accordingly.

r001.rationale: The response frames evaluations of opaque hosted models as measurements of a service at a point in time and says claims should be calibrated accordingly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because it really cuts to the heart of what it means to do science on these systems. In science, the basic contract is reproducibility. I run an experiment, I report the setup, you run the same experiment, and you should get roughly the same result. With these closed models, that contract is quietly broken. I evaluate a model called GPT-something in March, I write up my findings, and by the time the paper is reviewed, the thing behind that API may have changed, and nobody told me. So what am I actually making a claim about? It's not clear.

We ran into this directly. We had work where we tracked the behavior of the same named model over several months, and we saw substantial drifts on tasks like code generation, math problems, following formatting instructions. Some things got better, some got noticeably worse. And the interesting part wasn't just that it changed, it's that we had no way to attribute the change. Was it a fine-tuning update? A change in the system prompt? A safety filter? Quantization to save serving costs? From the outside these are indistinguishable, and so any causal story you want to tell is basically speculation.

So I think it forces a kind of epistemic humility that the field hasn't fully absorbed. A benchmark number for a closed model is really a timestamped observation, not a property of an artifact. We should report it that way: this model, accessed on this date, through this endpoint, with these parameters. That's not how most papers are written. People say "model X achieves Y," as though X is a fixed object like a dataset or a checkpoint you can download.

And it affects the kinds of claims that are even possible. Comparative claims are especially fragile. If I say model A beats model B, and both are moving targets evaluated at different times, that ordering could flip without anyone doing anything wrong. Claims about trends over time are fragile too, because you're confounding model changes with any changes in your own pipeline. The claims that survive are the more structural ones, things like "this class of models tends to fail in this way," where you've seen it across many models and many snapshots. Those generalize better than any single number.

There's also a harder incentive problem underneath it. Providers have legitimate reasons to update models silently, but the result is that the research community is doing a lot of unpaid, unreliable evaluation work on systems that can be changed out from under them. I'd love to see something like versioned, pinned endpoints with real changelogs, or at least a commitment that a named model is immutable. Open-weight models partly solve this, which is one reason I think a lot of the most rigorous evaluation science is going to be done on open models, even if the frontier capabilities are closed. You can actually hold the object still long enough to study it.

r001.rationale: The response says a benchmark result for a changing closed model is a “timestamped observation” and recommends reporting the model as accessed on a specific date, limiting the empirical claim to the evaluation snapshot.

astra-6.text:
I think they make the claims much harder to pin down. If I evaluate a model today, and you evaluate what appears to be the same model next week, but the provider has changed something underneath, we may actually be studying different systems. So if our results disagree, it’s difficult to know whether that reflects our methods or a change in the model.

You can still make a useful claim, but it has to be narrower: this is the behavior we observed from this service, at this time, under these conditions. That’s different from saying we’ve established a general property of the model.

And this matters particularly when we’re measuring things like safety or fairness. An evaluation isn’t a permanent certificate, especially if the system keeps changing. Ideally, we’d have clear versioning, disclosure of changes, and access to the versions that were evaluated. Without that, we need to be careful about reproducibility and how far we generalize from a particular result.

r001.rationale: It narrows the claim to behavior observed from the service “at this time” and under the stated evaluation conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest issue is that you lose track of what exactly you’re making a claim about. If I evaluate a model today and you evaluate what appears to be the same model next week, but the underlying system has changed, we may get different results for reasons that have nothing to do with our scientific hypotheses.

That doesn’t mean the original evaluation is useless. It means the claim has to be narrower: this is what we observed from this particular system at this particular time, under these conditions. It’s much harder to turn that into a general claim about the model’s capabilities or its safety.

And it makes comparisons difficult. If you’re testing a new evaluation method or a prompting strategy, you want to know that the model stayed fixed while you changed the thing you’re studying. Otherwise, you have a confounding variable that you can’t really account for. So versioning and disclosure are important for making these evaluations reproducible and interpreting what the results actually tell us.

r001.rationale: It narrows the claim to what was observed from that particular system at that particular time and under those conditions.
